assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, via Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and Ye's strontium clocks, reduced fractional clock uncertainty to the 1e-18 level and opened a new regime for precision metrology, relativistic geodesy and tests of fundamental constants. The discovery is clear, original and has demonstrably changed the field of atomic precision measurement.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed and first realised the magic-wavelength lattice scheme; Ye's group drove the accuracy and stability records and the many-body (spin-polarised Fermi gas) clock work. A two-person prize is clean and fits the supplied credit. Other groups (e.g. at PTB, NIST, SYRTE) contributed substantially but are not in the credited names.
assessment.maturity: Mature: independent clocks in several laboratories agree below 1e-18, and comparisons are routine. Recognition is timely; the 2005 prize covered frequency combs, which this builds on but does not duplicate.
uncertainties: How the committee should weigh the many other strontium/ytterbium clock groups against the two credited names.
Whether a future redefinition of the SI second would be a more natural time for recognition is uncertain.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposals for trapped-ion quantum gates and for quantum simulation with cold atoms and ions supplied the theoretical blueprint for two major experimental platforms and shaped modern quantum information science. Originality and lasting influence are very high.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller are the decisive joint authors of the 1995 gate proposal and of the follow-on optical-lattice and quantum-simulation ideas. A two-name prize is straightforward. Experimental realisation (Wineland, Blatt and others) is distinct and partly already recognised in 2012.
assessment.maturity: Mature: ion-trap gates and atomic simulators are now commercial and academic workhorses, and the theory has been confirmed repeatedly and independently.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 prize (Wineland) and with experimental credit for the realisations could raise fairness questions.
I note my own field proximity; I have no documented collaboration with either name that I am aware of.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Bistritzer-MacDonald flat-band prediction and the 2018 discovery of correlated insulators and superconductivity in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene opened moire quantum materials, a new and very active platform for correlated physics. The idea is original and the experimental follow-through decisive.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald made the theoretical prediction of the magic angle; Jarillo-Herrero's group made the decisive experimental discovery. The three names form a natural theory-plus-experiment configuration. Others (e.g. Cao, Fatemi, Dean, Yazdani and the Kim group) contributed, so credit is not exhaustive.
assessment.maturity: Reasonably mature but young: reproduced widely, though the origin of the superconductivity is still debated. Recognition may be somewhat early for the superconducting part, less so for the flat-band and moire concept.
uncertainties: Pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is unresolved.
Whether the first author Yuan Cao or other experimentalists should share credit is not decided by the supplied names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators, and its first experimental realisation in HgTe quantum wells, created a field of topological quantum matter. The concept is clear, original and has had wide impact on materials and quantum technology.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the decisive theoretical prediction; Molenkamp's group, building on the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, demonstrated the effect. The credited 3D-materials work of Hasan is separate and an allocation to three names necessarily omits Hasan, as well as theorists such as Zhang and Bernevig who are not in the credited names. This is a real allocation difficulty.
assessment.maturity: Mature: the effect is confirmed in multiple systems and the 3D case by ARPES, though practical applications remain modest. The 2016 prize recognised topological phase transitions, so partial overlap exists.
uncertainties: Exclusion of Hasan (3D topological insulators) and of Bernevig/Hughes/Zhang from the three-name configuration.
Degree of overlap with the 2016 Nobel Prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: BB84 and Ekert's entanglement-based protocol established quantum key distribution, linking quantum foundations to secure communication. The ideas are original and conceptually deep, with a large practical and theoretical legacy.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard are the clear originators of BB84; Ekert independently introduced the entanglement-based E91 protocol. The three-name credit fits well, though others (e.g. Wiesner on conjugate coding) have a historical claim.
assessment.maturity: Mature: QKD is experimentally demonstrated over fibre and satellite links, though large-scale practical security issues remain. The 2022 prize recognised related entanglement experiments, so timing is plausible but with some overlap.
uncertainties: Wiesner's early conjugate-coding idea and its relation to BB84 credit.
Practical deployment and side-channel security are not a measure of the physics but may colour perceptions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit quantum electrodynamics demonstrated strong coupling of superconducting qubits to microwave photons and underpins superconducting quantum processors. It is a clear and fundamental platform concept with strong theoretical and experimental backing.
assessment.attribution: The decisive contributions are the Blais et al. 2004 proposal and the Wallraff et al. 2004 experiment, with Schoelkopf's group leading the circuit design and later developments. Girvin is a co-author of the theory and is not selected here, which is a genuine allocation difficulty with four credited names.
assessment.maturity: Mature in the sense of widespread adoption, but the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits is close in subject, so timing is arguable.
uncertainties: Closeness to the 2025 prize and the omission of Girvin.
Whether the platform is regarded as a distinct discovery or as an engineering extension of earlier circuit experiments.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum error correction and topological fault tolerance are the theoretical basis for scalable quantum computing, showing that decoherence can in principle be controlled. The work is original and foundational for quantum information.
assessment.attribution: Shor's 1995 code, Steane's independent code and Kitaev's toric-code/anyon proposals are all decisive. The credited trio is plausible, but other contributors (Calderbank, Gottesman, Knill, Laflamme) have a strong claim that this configuration does not capture.
assessment.maturity: Experimental demonstrations of below-threshold error correction are very recent, so validation is real but still developing; the theory is mature, the physical vindication is partial.
uncertainties: Large credit-allocation uncertainty among several authors of QEC codes.
Whether recent experimental demonstrations are enough to establish physical maturity.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: IceCube's discovery of a diffuse flux of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos and the association of one source with a blazar founded neutrino astronomy at TeV-PeV energies. The result is clearly important and an experimental breakthrough.
assessment.attribution: Halzen led the conception of IceCube; Karle and Yoshida had major roles in the instrument and analysis, but the collaboration is very large and individual attribution is difficult. The supplied credit supports a prize configuration only loosely.
assessment.maturity: Reasonably mature given independent observations such as the Galactic-plane neutrino map, though the source population is still open.
uncertainties: Attribution within a very large collaboration.
The astrophysical source origin remains largely undetermined.
